lessons.title: Local Government Debt and What China's Slowdown Means for India

body.text: China's biggest debt problem is not one developer. It is a network of local government companies that borrowed against land prices, and when land stopped selling, the bill landed on the whole economy. A slower China reshapes India's risks and opportunities at the same time.

children.text: On 8 November 2024, China's top legislature approved a 10 trillion yuan programme to help local governments swap their so-called hidden debts for cheaper, officially recognised bonds. It was a quiet admission of a problem that had been building for more than a decade: the companies set up by Chinese cities and provinces to build roads, bridges and industrial parks had borrowed on a scale that some estimates put above half of China's GDP.

The previous two lessons covered China's markets and its property developers. This final China lesson follows the money to local governments, explains why economists worry about a Japan-style lost decade, and shows what all of it means for Indian investors.

body.caption: China's local debt problem on the five-stage map

cells: Build-up
Local governments fund infrastructure through off-budget companies, repaid largely by selling land to developers at rising prices
Trigger
The property crash from 2021 collapses land sales, the main source of repayment
Panic and recognition
Slow, not sudden: local governments cut spending, delay payments and roll over debt, while prices across the economy fall
Policy response
A 10 trillion yuan debt swap announced in November 2024, plus pressure on banks to extend and refinance local loans
Repair and recovery
Still under way: the swap buys time, but land revenue has not recovered and growth depends on new sources

children.text: Build-up: How Chinese Cities Borrowed Against Land
Chinese local governments were expected to deliver fast growth and build infrastructure, but for years they faced strict limits on borrowing directly. Their workaround was the
local government financing vehicle
, or LGFV.

markDefs.definition: A company set up by a Chinese city or province to borrow money and build infrastructure off the government's own books. Its debts are widely assumed to be backed by the local government, even when they are not officially counted as government debt.

children.text: A city sets up an LGFV and transfers land to it as capital.
The LGFV borrows from banks and bond investors, using the land and the city's implied backing as security.
It builds roads, metro lines, industrial parks and housing-related infrastructure.
The city sells nearby land to property developers at rising prices.
Land sale revenue, directly or indirectly, helps repay and roll over the LGFV's debt.
The whole system rested on land prices. By 2021, land sale revenue made up about 30% of total local government revenue, and land sales plus land-related taxes together made up about 38%.

body.title: Chinese local governments' land sale revenue

children.text: The fall did not stop there. Land sale revenue dropped a further 16% in 2024 as the property slump continued.

body.title: What a Land Slump Does to a City Budget
body.prompt: A Chinese city collects 100 billion yuan of revenue a year, of which 30% comes from land sales. If land sale revenue falls by half and all other revenue stays the same, by what percentage does the city's total revenue fall?
body.explanation: Land revenue = 30% × 100 billion = 30 billion yuan. Halving it removes 15 billion yuan. Total revenue falls from 100 billion to 85 billion yuan, a 15% drop. The city still has the same salaries, services and LGFV debts to support, so it must cut spending, delay payments to contractors, or borrow more. Multiply that across thousands of local governments and it becomes a nationwide drag on growth.

body.title: Go deeper: why LGFV debt is so hard to measure

children.text: Estimates of LGFV debt vary widely because much of it sits in layers of companies. The IMF put it at about 65 trillion yuan in 2024, while other estimates from banks and researchers range from 50 to 90 trillion yuan, roughly 40% to 72% of China's GDP.

One reason is a pyramid structure. An LGFV can borrow money, inject it as capital into a subsidiary, and that subsidiary can then borrow again against its new capital. Each layer makes the group look better capitalised than it really is. It is the same problem you saw with IL&FS and its web of more than 250 group companies in India, only on a vastly larger scale.
Policy Response: The 10 Trillion Yuan Swap
Beijing's answer was not a bailout that wiped debts away. It was a swap: replacing expensive, hidden LGFV debt with cheaper, official local government bonds, spreading repayments over many years.

body.caption: The debt swap programme announced on 8 November 2024

cells: Higher local government debt ceiling
6 trillion yuan
Allowed over three years, at 2 trillion yuan a year, to refinance hidden debt
Special bond quota
4 trillion yuan
800 billion yuan a year for five years, from 2024 to 2028, set aside for debt swaps
Official target
Hidden debt from 14.3 trillion yuan to 2.3 trillion yuan
Reduction targeted by 2028, using the swap and other measures

body.text: A swap lowers interest costs and reduces the risk of a disorderly default, the same logic as the Brady Plan of 1989 in Chapter 2 and India's evergreening concerns in Chapter 1. But it does not make the debt disappear, and it does nothing on its own to restore land sales. Markets were disappointed that it was not paired with bigger direct support for spending.

children.text: The Bigger Fear: Deflation and a Lost Decade

With developers failing, local governments squeezed and households cautious, prices across China's economy stopped rising. China's GDP deflator, a broad measure of prices across everything the economy produces, stayed negative for 12 consecutive quarters until the first quarter of 2026, before turning positive in the second quarter. Consumer price inflation averaged 0% in 2025, far below the government's target.
Falling prices sound good for buyers, but for a heavily indebted economy they are dangerous. As you learnt with Irving Fisher's
debt deflation
in Chapter 2, when prices and incomes fall, debts fixed in money terms become heavier.

markDefs.definition: A spiral in which falling prices increase the real burden of fixed debts, causing defaults and spending cuts that push prices down further.

body.title: Japan after 1990 vs China in the 2020s

columns.label: Japan after its 1990 bubble
points: Property and stock prices collapse after a credit-fuelled boom
Banks slow to recognise bad loans and keep weak borrowers alive
Years of weak growth and falling prices, the "lost decade"
A heavily indebted private sector focuses on repaying debt instead of spending

columns.label: China in the 2020s
points: Property prices, sales and investment fall for years after 2021
Local debts rolled over and swapped rather than written off
A long run of negative GDP deflator readings until 2026
Households cautious after losing wealth in property

children.text: Many economists call this risk "Japanification". China is not identical to Japan: it is still much poorer per person, with more room to grow, and its government controls far more of the banking system. But the ingredients of a long, slow grind, rather than a sudden crash, are clearly visible.

children.text: What China's Slowdown Means for India
India is exposed to China less through financial links, since Indian banks and investors hold little Chinese debt, and more through trade, manufacturing and commodities.

body.caption: The channels from China's slowdown to India

cells: Trade and dumping
Weak demand at home pushes Chinese producers to sell surplus goods abroad at low prices
India imposed a safeguard duty of 12% on certain flat steel imports from 21 April 2025, tapering over three years
Import dependence
India relies on China for electronics, batteries, solar cells and industrial inputs
Imports from China reached $113.46 billion in 2024-25, and the trade deficit hit $99.2 billion
China plus one
Global companies diversify manufacturing away from China
India's iPhone exports reached about ₹2 trillion in 2025-26, over three quarters of its smartphone exports
Commodities
Weaker Chinese construction means lower demand for steel, iron ore, coal and other raw materials
Cheaper raw materials help Indian manufacturers and importers, but squeeze metal producers' prices
Capital flows
Global investors reallocate within emerging markets
Money leaving China can flow towards India, but a China shock can also hit all emerging markets at once, as in August 2015

body.title: Opportunity or Threat?
body.question: Chinese steelmakers, facing weak demand from their own collapsing construction sector, export large volumes of cheap steel. Which Indian group is most directly threatened, and which benefits?
options: Threatened: Indian steel producers. Benefits: Indian companies that use steel, such as makers of machinery and appliances
Threatened: Indian IT services companies. Benefits: Indian banks
Threatened: Indian steel users. Benefits: Indian steel producers
Neither group is affected, because steel is not traded internationally
body.explanation: Cheap imported steel undercuts Indian steel producers on price, which is why India imposed a safeguard duty in 2025. At the same time, companies that buy steel as a raw material benefit from lower costs. The same shock creates winners and losers, and policy decides how the balance is struck.

body.label: India's Guardrail on Chinese Investment
body.value: Press Note 3, April 2020, eased in March 2026
body.context: From April 2020, all foreign direct investment from countries sharing a land border with India, including China, needed government approval, to prevent opportunistic takeovers during the pandemic. On 10 March 2026, the Cabinet eased the rule: non-controlling beneficial ownership of up to 10% can now come in through the automatic route, subject to sectoral caps, and a 60-day timeline applies to certain approvals in sectors such as electronic components and capital goods, where Indian ownership and control is retained.

body.title: Name the Borrower
body.textWithBlank: Companies set up by Chinese cities and provinces to borrow off the government's books are called local government financing ___.
body.explanation: Local government financing vehicles, or LGFVs. Their debt is the hidden centre of China's debt problem, closely tied to land prices and the property crisis.

body.title: Reading the China Story as an Indian Investor
body.scenario: A friend says, "China's economy is in trouble, so India is the obvious winner. Every Indian manufacturing stock will benefit, and there is no downside for us."
body.prompt: Using this chapter, explain where your friend has a point, where the argument is too simple, and what you would actually track.
body.modelAnswer: Where the friend has a point: global companies diversifying away from China have brought real manufacturing investment to India, with iPhone exports reaching about ₹2 trillion in 2025-26, and weaker Chinese demand for raw materials can lower input costs for Indian industry. Where it is too simple: first, not every sector gains. Cheap Chinese exports can hurt Indian producers of steel, chemicals, solar equipment and other goods, which is why India has used safeguard and anti-dumping duties. Second, India still depends heavily on Chinese inputs, with a $99.2 billion trade deficit in 2024-25, so disruptions in China can raise Indian costs. Third, a China shock can hit all emerging markets at once, as the Sensex fall of 1,624 points in August 2015 showed. Fourth, a rising stock price may already reflect the China plus one story, so the opportunity does not automatically make a particular company a good investment. What to track: company-level evidence of new export orders and capacity, not just the headline story; India's trade data with China; trade remedy decisions such as safeguard duties; China's property and land sales data and its price indicators such as the GDP deflator; and foreign portfolio flows into India when China-related news hits markets. The lesson is that China's slowdown creates both winners and losers in India, and the details matter more than the headline.

cards.definition: A local government financing vehicle: a company set up by a Chinese city or province to borrow and build infrastructure off the government's books.
Local governments funding spending and debt repayments by selling land to developers. Land sales made up about 30% of local revenue in 2021.
Replacing expensive hidden debt with cheaper official bonds, like China's 10 trillion yuan programme in November 2024.
A broad measure of prices across everything an economy produces. China's was negative for 12 straight quarters until early 2026.
The risk of a long period of weak growth, falling prices and debt repair after a bubble, as Japan experienced after 1990.
Companies adding manufacturing in another country, such as India, to reduce dependence on China.

points: Chinese local governments borrowed through LGFVs, with debt estimated by the IMF at about 65 trillion yuan in 2024, much of it backed by expected land sales
Land sale revenue fell from 8.7 trillion yuan in 2021 to 5.8 trillion in 2023 and dropped a further 16% in 2024, breaking the repayment model
Beijing responded with a 10 trillion yuan debt swap in November 2024, which buys time and cuts interest costs but does not remove the debt or revive land sales
A 12-quarter run of negative GDP deflator readings until early 2026 raised fears of Japan-style debt deflation and a lost decade
For India, China's slowdown brings both opportunities, such as China plus one manufacturing and cheaper raw materials, and threats, such as dumping, import dependence and emerging market contagion

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice. The city budget exercise and the investor scenario are hypothetical, and no company, sector or fund is being recommended. Estimates of Chinese local government debt vary widely, and Chinese economic data continue to change. Figures are drawn from IMF, Chinese government, Indian government and other public sources.
